transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12 16:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Evan (Nyx Head of ML), Priya (Nyx Infra), Martin (Nyx CTO)

Summary (auto-generated): Discussed p95 targets (50-150ms for critical flows), concurrency (up to 250 concurrent streams), streaming token throughput and benchmarking approach. Next steps include pricing, security docs, and a 1-week benchmark.

00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood, i'll hand over to liam for the technical walk and then we'll do q and a.
00:18 Evan: thanks, maya, appreciate it, quick intros from our side — i'm evan, head of ml at nyx, priya is infra, martin is cto — we wanna understand latency/throughput tradeoffs before committing to a pilot.
00:35 Priya: hi, everyone — our main thing is p95 under load for live scoring, ideal < 150ms for short completions, and about 50-100ms for micro prompts, also we use streaming heavily.
00:50 Liam: got it. can you share typical prompt lengths and tokens/sec expectations?
00:58 Evan: baseline prompt size averages 20-40 tokens, but some multi-turn summaries hit 300-800 tokens. Our product has two paths: real-time scoring (user-facing) and async batch enrichment. The realtime path needs streaming with low tail latency.
01:15 Martin: also data rules — must be able to run in our VPC or private deployment for certain customers. SOC2 is table stakes.
01:30 Maya: that helps. just to orient, nyx is deciding between redwood hosted for faster onboarding, dedicated reserved pools for predictability, or private for customers requiring on-prem/VPC. we'd recommend starting with hosted or dedicated depending on traffic but we can scope private too.
01:50 Evan: ok, show me numbers — p95 is the thing. what p95 can you hit for a 7B-ish model, and up to 70B with quantization?
02:05 Liam: so typical profiles — on our hosted tier we see p95 around 80-120ms for 7B models at single-shot 40 token responses with low concurrency. For higher concurrency and larger models it increases; dedicated capacity lets you pin GPU pools which gives predictable p95 and throughput. For 70B quant, p95 is more like 300-800ms depending on sequence length and whether kv-cache hits are warm.
02:35 Evan: kv-cache hits? can you explain — we do lots of repeated prefixes.
02:40 Liam: sure, the runtime keeps key-value cache across requests for same session so if you're doing multi-turn it avoids recomputing the prefix which reduces per-token latency. cold starts vs warm cache can be 2-3x difference sometimes.
03:05 Priya: and batching? we want high tokens/sec for batch jobs.
03:10 Liam: batching increases throughput (tokens/sec) but adds latency; we do continuous batching with dynamic thresholds to balance SLOs. you can tune batching window and max batch size per route.
03:25 Evan: what about streaming? do you support chunked token streaming with backpressure?
03:30 Liam: yes, streaming is supported both on hosted and dedicated, including chunked updates, and we support client-side and server-side flow control — but tail p95 for the first token is what users care about for interactive experiences.
03:48 Martin: can we get concrete concurrency numbers? we expect peaks of 200-250 concurrent real-time connections, and spikes to 800 for a few minutes during peak trading hours.
04:00 Liam: for 200-250 concurrent low-latency streams we'd recommend dedicated capacity — you can reserve enough instances to keep p95 in your target. For spikes we offer burst capacity or cross-region fallback to keep service up.
04:18 Evan: any examples of tokens/sec on dedicated for, say, 13B model with q4 quant?
04:25 Liam: on a single dedicated GPU cluster, with q4 and batching tuned, you can get roughly 400-800 tokens/sec sustained for medium sequences. For higher token-per-second you scale horizontally of course.
04:40 Priya: those numbers seem optimistic; can you share benchmark artifacts?
04:44 Maya: yes, we'll share a benchmark spreadsheet and sample scripts — link in followup — there's an internal runbook our SEs use.
04:55 Evan: also, how do you measure p95? what about cold vs warm?
05:00 Liam: we provide both p50/p95/p99 across token latencies, and we annotate hot cache vs cold start. our benchmarking compares median token latency and time-to-first-token (TTFT). we can run your dataset to get representative numbers.
05:20 Martin: security: do you have SOC2, SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs?
05:27 Maya: yes — we are SOC2 Type II, support SAML/SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logging; we'll attach the compliance pack.
05:40 Priya: for private mode, how do upgrades and observability work?
05:44 Liam: private gives you control plane in your VPC; we can push upgrades via your change window and we expose the same console telemetry via secure links. logs can be forwarded to your S3 or SIEM.
06:05 Evan: ok, what does a PoC look like? we want a 1-week baseline where you run tests against our dataset and we compare hosted vs dedicated numbers.
06:15 Maya: typical POC is a week: first day onboarding & dataset transfer (S3), day 2-4 baseline runs and tuning, day 5 review and next steps. SE will run scripts, share scripts, and we sync on observed p95 and scaling behavior.
06:35 Evan: who pays for the initial benchmark infra? we don't want unexpected bills.
06:40 Maya: for initial benchmark we often cover some infra credits for hosted runs; dedicated runs usually require a small commitment but we can structure a short eval contract. we'll outline in the sheet.
06:55 Priya: latency target specifics — we have two SLAs: 1) fast path for trading alerts p95 < 120ms for responses up to 60 tokens; 2) conversation summarization p95 < 500ms for 800-token outputs is preferred but not strict.
07:15 Liam: noted. we'll prioritize the fast path tuning (smaller context, streaming) and show the tradeoffs for the longer summaries. quantization choices and model selection can hit those targets differently.
07:30 Evan: model variants — could you fallback to smaller models automatically?
07:34 Liam: yes, smart routing can fall back to a smaller model for lower-priority requests or when capacity is constrained; you can define policies by route.
07:50 Martin: network egress and region — we operate in us-east and eu-west; some customers require EU-only data.
07:58 Maya: regional routing is supported; for strict residency we'd recommend private deployment in eu-west or VPC with data residency controls.
08:10 Evan: okay, let's talk about benchmarking methodology — what scripts do you use and what metrics will you deliver?
08:17 Liam: we use a JMH-like load generator for token-level tests and a HTTP/streaming harness for interactive tests. metrics delivered: TTFT, per-token latency distribution, CPU/GPU utilization, memory (kv cache) hit rates, tokens/sec, and end-to-end p50/p95/p99. we'll annotate cold vs warm cache runs.
08:40 Priya: can we instrument our tracing (open telemetry) into your console for deeper correlation?
08:45 Liam: yes, we support traces via open telemetry exporters; we can ingest traces to correlate request spans with token latencies.
08:55 Evan: any gotchas with quantization — we heard q4 might degrade quality on some models.
09:00 Liam: quality regressions can happen; Redwood Optimize gives model/quant recommendations per workload and we encourage evals to verify quality vs perf. we'll help run evals for your prompt set.
09:18 Martin: timeline — we want to decide within 3-4 weeks and have pilot in next quarter.
09:24 Maya: that's reasonable. we'll target the POC within that window; we'll aim to return pricing and docs this week.
09:35 Evan: cool. priya, can you share expected concurrency profile and a traffic dump?
09:40 Priya: yes, i'll export a 48-hour capture and drop in the S3 link you provide.
09:46 Liam: perfect. for the bench we'll need a representative prompt set and the traffic shape including peak qps, percentiles, and streaming connection counts.
10:00 Evan: any clarification on metrics — do you report token/sec per GPU or per cluster?
10:05 Liam: we report both; single GPU throughput and cluster aggregated tokens/sec. we'll include breakdown by model variant and quantization.
10:15 Priya: curious about autoscaling — how fast can dedicated scale up for sudden spikes?
10:20 Liam: autoscaling is configurable; with reserved nodes we can do fast warmup using pre-warmed instances; typical scale-up to add nodes takes minutes (depends on region); for millisecond spikes we recommend burst capacity and routing fallbacks.
10:38 Evan: imperfect transcription note: last alliance maybe said kv cash earlier in the notes (laughs)
10:45 Maya: (laugh) yes, kv-cache — sorry the automated transcript sometimes garbles.
10:50 Liam: ok, let's walk through a sample bench scenario. assume 200 concurrent streams, average response 40 tokens, target p95 < 120ms. First token time budget is tight. We would run a warmup phase to saturate kv cache and then measure TTFT and tokens/sec.
11:20 Priya: do you support GPU affinity for dedicated pools? we want certain nodes pinned to particular customers.
11:26 Maya: yes, Dedicated allows tenant isolation and pinned GPU pools.
11:30 Martin: for private deployments — how does observability parity with hosted look? we need the same dashboards.
11:35 Liam: same console, metrics exported behind your network; some enterprise controls differ but we keep feature parity for metrics and alerts.
11:46 Evan: okay wrapping up, can you confirm deliverables?
11:50 Maya: sure — 1) pricing + Dedicated vs Hosted worksheet, 2) SOC2/ISO and VPC onboarding docs, 3) SE test scripts and benchmark plan, 4) Nyx to send traffic profile and prompt set. We'll schedule the benchmark kickoff for next week if you can provide the artifacts.
12:08 Evan: that works. any blockers from security? we'll route SOC questions to our compliance team.
12:12 Priya: i will loop in our security contact after this call.
12:18 Maya: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invite for the benchmark kickoff and share links.
12:30 Martin: thanks all.
12:35 Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcript had occasional mislabels and word swaps (kv-cache -> kv cash), some punctuation missing. This capture is medium quality and contains natural speech patterns and cross talk.

Recap (auto): Redwood to send pricing and docs; SE to run benchmark; Nyx to provide traffic and prompt set; follow-up call to review results; likely POC start next quarter.
